 A Married Couple Over 65 Can Take $47,500 Out of a 401(k) in 2026 and Pay $0 in Federal Tax. The New $12,000 Senior Deduction Is Why
 Gerelyn Terzo Tue, November 3, 2026 at 3:03 PM PST 6 min read Quick Read 
 A married couple over 65 with no other income can withdraw $47,500 from a 401(k) in 2026 and owe $0 in federal tax. 
 Three stacked deductions fully offset the $47,500 withdrawal: a $32,200 standard deduction, a $3,300 age add-on, and a new $12,000 senior deduction. 
 The zero-tax math breaks once Social Security begins, as benefits start becoming taxable when combined income exceeds $32,000 for joint filers. 
 The biggest 401k decisions tend to get made once and never revisited: when to roll it over, what to hold inside it, and when to start taking money out. That is exactly what the report: 401k & IRA Tips and Answers was created to address, and it is free today. Read more here . (Sponsor) 
 A married couple, both 66, have a large traditional 401(k) and a simple plan for 2026. They will withdraw $47,500 to cover living expenses and have no other income. That means no pension, no wages and no Social Security yet. Under 2026 rules, that withdrawal produces $0 in federal income tax. The tax code makes that possible. 
 StockPhotoDirectors / Shutterstock.com Three Deductions Stack Up to $47,500 
 The first layer is the regular standard deduction, which rises to $32,200 for married couples filing jointly in 2026. The second is the additional deduction for taxpayers 65 or older: $1,650 per person, or $3,300 for the couple. 
 The third layer is new. The One Big Beautiful Bill created a deduction of $6,000 for each qualified individual for tax years 2025 to 2028. Two spouses over 65 together claim $12,000. 
 Added together, the three layers shelter $47,500. Take a $47,500 401(k) distribution, subtract $47,500 in deductions, and taxable income is zero. That pretax money was never taxed going in. This year it never gets taxed coming out. 
 Four Conditions Decide Who Gets the Senior Deduction 
 The older age-65 add-on is easy to claim. The new deduction has more rules:

 Age: each spouse counts only if they turn 65 before the close of the taxable year. If one spouse is 64, the couple gets half the benefit. 
 Filing status: married taxpayers get it only if they file a joint return. Filing separately means losing it completely. Couples who split returns for other reasons should check what that costs them. 
 Identification: the return has to include each qualifying spouse's Social Security number. A taxpayer ID number issued in place of an SSN doesn't count. 
 Income: each $6,000 shrinks by 6% of modified adjusted gross income above $150,000 on a joint return. Big Roth conversions or capital gains can cut into it. 
 Story Continues Withdrawals Above Zero Still Come Cheap 
 That $47,500 is the tax-free limit for our couple. Couples with large balances should look at what comes after it. The 10% bracket covers the first $24,800 of joint taxable income. That means a withdrawal of $72,300 is taxed at no more than 10% on any dollar. 
 The 12% bracket runs up to $100,800 of taxable income. Withdrawing $148,300 fills that bracket and still stays under the $150,000 phaseout, so the full senior deduction survives. Federal tax on that withdrawal comes to about $11,600, an effective rate near 8%. 
 Medicare surcharges shouldn't be a concern at that level either. The first 2026 income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA) surcharge for joint filers applies only above $218,000. IRMAA looks back two years, so income in 2026 generally sets premiums for 2028, using that year's thresholds. Money left in the 401(k) will eventually come out as required distributions stacked on top of Social Security. 
 Paying 10% or 12% on it now could be better than paying 22% or more on top of a benefit check later. These silent years between the last paycheck and the first RMD are the exact window. We sized it up in a free Roth conversion guide. 
 Social Security Breaks the Zero-Tax Math 
 The $0 result only works with no other taxable income. Benefits start becoming taxable once half your benefits plus all other income goes over $32,000 if married filing jointly. In 2026, the average senior couple collects about $3,208 a month. 
 Add six months of those checks to a $47,500 withdrawal, and combined income reaches $57,124, well above the $32,000 threshold. Part of their Social Security becomes taxable, and the three deductions no longer cover all their income. Pensions, interest and part-time wages can also eat into that tax-free room. The $47,500 figure works for couples with no other income. 
 How to Use the 2026 Window 
 Time withdrawals around when you claim Social Security. Couples between 65 and 70 who are delaying benefits get their cheapest chance to draw down pretax savings. Each year of waiting also raises the future check. 
 Choose a target bracket first, then size the withdrawal or Roth conversion to fit it. Use $47,500 for zero federal tax. Use $72,300 to stay at 10%, or $148,300 to fill the 12% bracket and keep the full senior deduction. Your state may tax the same dollars. 
 Keep the deadline in mind. The senior deduction applies only to taxable years beginning before January 1, 2029, so after 2026 only 2027 and 2028 remain. Each year without a planned withdrawal is one less year of the deduction you can use.
